# Recall



* Writing is  __learned__
  * But certain aspects of  __computer\-mediated communication __ \(CMC\) seem like they are acquired
  * Emojis as extralinguistic material \(like facial expressions and body language\)
* What makes the digital environment different from face\-to\-face?
* __Computational linguistics __ is the area of linguistics that applies the methods of computer science to the analysis of language and speech
  * Speech synthesis and speech recognition
  * Not easy problems\!\!
  * Accuracy and speed

---


# But also…

![](images/20-How%20do%20computers%20help%20with%20language_1.png)

Computers are stupid\.


---




* Our focus before was on  __speech recognition__ \, and we spent our time discussing mostly how  __sounds __ were processed and turned into text that a computer could understand
  * But that “understanding” boiled down to 1s and 0s
  * And it relied on the devices being talked to having sets of standard commands \(“call Mom”\) and built\-in probabilities that it could use to decipher what you intended
* So\, is it really “understanding” language?
  * We’re talking about  __natural language processing__
  * The answer to this lies in understanding the complexity of human grammar
  * And\, in fact\, computers are a still not great on the morphosyntactic properties of language\!

* What is syntax?
  * “The way in which words are put together to form phrases and sentences\.” \(American Heritage Dictionary\)
  * It’s all about structure and rules\!
* Remember\, in order to talk about sentence structure\, we need to know a little about  __parts of speech__ \, or categories of words based on similar meanings\, forms\, and functions
* __You know these\! But it’s not always unambiguous…__

# 2. Word order is important

![](images/20-How%20do%20computers%20help%20with%20language_5.jpg)



* It affects grammaticality and meaning\.
  * Mary dumped John\. ≠ John dumped Mary\.
  * \*John Mary dumped\.
  * \*Dumped Mary John\.
* Languages differ in word order
::: {.notes}

Word order is more flexible in some languages compared to English, particularly languages that heavily inflect for case.


:::


---


# Word Order

![](images/20-How%20do%20computers%20help%20with%20language_6.png)



* We usually talk about word order in terms of grammatical roles like subject \(S\)\, object \(O\)\, and verb \(V\)
* These pieces are combined in different ways
  * SVO\, SOV\, VSO\, VOS\, OSV\, OVS
  * For example\, Irish and Welsh are VSO
  * Siaradodd 	Aled 	y 	Gymraeg\.
      * spoke		Aled	DEF	Welsh
      * Verb		Subject	Object
      * “Aled spoke Welsh\.”
* Almost no languages use OSV or OVS
  * However\, every language has  _some_  rules about word order\.

# Constituency

![](images/20-How%20do%20computers%20help%20with%20language_7.png)



* We are trying to show that certain words clump together into groups – and even these groups clump together into bigger and bigger groups\.
* So\, we have to think about grammar as being hierarchical
  * Like a tree rather than like a line


![](images/20-How%20do%20computers%20help%20with%20language_8.png)


---


# 4. Constituents form a hierarchical structure

![](images/20-How%20do%20computers%20help%20with%20language_9.jpg)



* __Each node is equivalent to a constituent\!__
    * Everything that hangs below a node \(directly or indirectly\) is  _inside_  that particular constituent\, and nothing else\.
    * One word can belong to several different \(bigger and bigger\) constituents at different levels\.

---


# Why hierarchical?



* All utterances are said or written in a  _linear_  mode\.
* This can lead to ambiguity…
  * Yoko Ono will talk about her husband John Lennon who was killed in an interview with Barbara Walters\.
  * How is this ambiguous?


![](images/20-How%20do%20computers%20help%20with%20language_10.png)

![](images/20-How%20do%20computers%20help%20with%20language_11.png)

![](images/20-How%20do%20computers%20help%20with%20language_15.jpg)

# Ambiguity



* The sentence has 2 meanings:
  * a\) Sarah saw \[a man with a telescope\]\. = the man was holding a telescope
  * b\) Sarah saw \[a man\] \[with a telescope\]\. = she used a telescope to see him
* Diagramming the sentences’ underlying hierarchical structure can disambiguate the meaning\.

---




* In the scene from  _2001: A Space Odyssey\, _ HAL says\, “I’m sorry\, Dave\. I’m afraid I can’t do that”
  * This requires a level of understanding of “Open the pod bay doors\, HAL\.” that computers just don’t have\!
  * All the stuff we’ve said about syntax today is stuff you do automatically\!
  * To be able to  __parse\, __ or break down a sentence into its component parts so that the meaning of the sentence can be understood\, a computer would need to \(at least\) know:
    * Meanings of the words and word order
    * What makes a sentence \(specifically an imperative\, or command\, one\)
    * How to respond to imperatives \(that they have never encountered and are not likely in the database\)


# How is this about computers?


---


# Help me, HAL!

![](images/20-How%20do%20computers%20help%20with%20language_17.jpg)



* And\, in addition to that\, to be able respond in this way\, a computer would need to:
  * Recognize that “I’m afraid” can mean something like “I’m sorry” not just “I have fear”
  * That using something like “I’m afraid” would be acceptable/appropriate here
  * Be able to not just execute the command \(=free will?\!\)
  * Refer to the asker by name
  * And so much more\!
* We’ve done better with speech recognition than with true linguistic processing\!
  * For a computer to understand meaning\, we have to give it a lot more than algorithms and probabilities\!
  * “Simple\-minded definitions will give the wrong results\.” \(p\. 107\)
